chapters.title: Chapter 5: Central Banks in Crisis, and What Investors Learn

lessons.title: Demonetisation 2016: Liquidity Shock and the Banking System

body.text: On a Tuesday evening in November 2016, 86% of India's cash stopped being money. Demonetisation was not a monetary policy decision, but it ran straight through the banking system, and it left the RBI managing the biggest liquidity flood in its history. It is the clearest example in this course of how currency management, liquidity tools and bank balance sheets are all connected.

children.text: The last two lessons covered crises that arrived from outside India. This one was made at home. Whatever you think of its aims, demonetisation is a remarkable case study in what happens when a central bank has to absorb, rather than inject, an enormous amount of liquidity, all at once.
What Happened on 8 November 2016

In a televised address, the Prime Minister announced that ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes would cease to be legal tender from midnight. The stated aims were to attack black money, counterfeit notes and terror financing. People could deposit or exchange old notes at banks over the following weeks.

body.text: This lesson looks only at the monetary and market mechanics. Whether demonetisation achieved its stated goals remains politically contested, and that debate is outside the scope of this course. What is not in dispute is how it moved cash, deposits and bond yields.

children.text: The Cash Crunch and the Rules That Followed

events.title: Announcement
events.description: ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes cease to be legal tender. ATM withdrawals are initially capped at ₹2,000 a day, with a weekly limit of ₹24,000 from savings accounts.

events.title: Incremental CRR of 100%
events.description: Banks must hold 100% CRR on the increase in their deposits between 16 September and 11 November, impounding the flood of new deposits.

events.title: MSS ceiling raised
events.description: The government raises the Market Stabilisation Scheme limit from ₹30,000 crore to ₹6 lakh crore, so the RBI can absorb liquidity with interest-paying bonds instead.

events.title: RBI surprises with a hold
events.description: Governor Urjit Patel keeps the repo rate at 6.25% despite widespread expectations of a cut, citing uncertainty from demonetisation and US rate hikes, and announces the incremental CRR will be withdrawn from 10 December.

events.title: Weekly cap raised
events.description: The weekly savings account limit rises to ₹50,000.

events.title: All limits removed
events.description: Normal cash withdrawals resume, four months after the announcement.

children.text: The Banking System Floods

Think about what happens mechanically. Households and businesses had to bring cash to banks. Cash that had been sitting outside the banking system became bank deposits. The RBI's own assessment put the surge in aggregate deposits at about ₹6.72 lakh crore.
People deposit old ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes into their accounts.
Bank deposits, and therefore NDTL, jump, while cash in circulation collapses.
Banks cannot lend that money quickly, because credit demand has not risen and the economy is slowing.
Banks park the money in government securities and with the RBI, so demand for G-Secs soars.
Bond prices rise and yields fall sharply, exactly as you would expect from Chapter 3.

body.text: This is Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 running in reverse. Normally the RBI worries about injecting liquidity. Here it faced the opposite problem: far too much money inside the banking system, with no productive home for it, pushing market rates down and threatening its control over policy.

body.title: Why Did Bond Yields Fall?
body.question: After demonetisation, Indian government bond yields dropped sharply. What is the main explanation?
options: The RBI cut the repo rate aggressively in November 2016
Banks were flooded with new deposits they could not lend, so they bought government bonds, pushing prices up and yields down
Foreign investors bought Indian bonds heavily
The government stopped issuing new bonds
body.explanation: The RBI actually held the repo rate at 6.25% in December 2016. Yields fell because banks suddenly had a huge pile of deposits and weak loan demand, so they bought government securities. More demand means higher prices and lower yields, the seesaw you learned in Chapter 3.

children.text: Why the RBI Used an Incremental CRR

markDefs.definition: A temporary requirement that banks hold a much higher cash reserve ratio, here 100%, on the growth in their deposits over a specific period, used to absorb a sudden surge in liquidity.

children.text: With so much cash in the system, overnight rates risked falling far below the repo rate, which would have undermined the RBI's control over monetary policy. The RBI first reached for the bluntest tool available: an
incremental CRR
of 100% on the deposit growth between 16 September and 11 November 2016. Estimates at the time put the amount impounded at around ₹3.5 lakh crore.

body.title: What Did the Incremental CRR Cost Banks?
body.prompt: Suppose about ₹3,50,000 crore of deposits were impounded under the 100% incremental CRR, which pays no interest. If banks could otherwise have earned 6.25% a year on that money, how much interest did they forgo over one 14-day reporting fortnight, in ₹ crore? Round to the nearest crore.
body.explanation: ₹3,50,000 crore × 6.25% × 14 ÷ 365 = about ₹839 crore for a single fortnight. That is why the measure was explicitly temporary. Within two weeks the government raised the MSS ceiling to ₹6 lakh crore so the RBI could absorb the same liquidity using bonds that actually pay banks interest, and the incremental CRR was withdrawn from 10 December 2016.

body.title: Two Ways to Soak Up a Liquidity Flood

columns.label: Incremental CRR
points: Immediate, can be imposed in days
Pays banks no interest at all
Suitable only as an emergency stopgap

columns.label: Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS)
points: Takes longer to set up, needs a government ceiling
Banks receive interest on the bonds they hold
Cost is borne by the government, not the banks

children.text: How Markets Reacted

The announcement coincided with Donald Trump's US election victory, so 9 November 2016 brought a double shock. The Sensex plunged as much as 6.1% during the day before recovering to close about 339 points lower. The deeper damage came over the following weeks, as investors weighed the hit to consumption. The Nifty slid to around 7,900 by late December 2016, a seven-month low, before a strong recovery through 2017 that took it roughly 29% above that level.

children.text: The Longer-Term Effects
Growth slowed.
Estimates vary, but studies and contemporary assessments put the hit to GDP growth at up to about 1.5 percentage points in the affected quarters, concentrated in cash-intensive and informal sectors.
Digital payments accelerated.
Digital payments rose about 55% in 2016-17. UPI, launched only months before demonetisation, went from about 2 crore transactions in FY17 to over 24,000 crore transactions in FY26.
Cash came back.
Currency in circulation was about ₹42.85 lakh crore on 31 August 2026, far above the ₹17.97 lakh crore before demonetisation.

body.title: How Much Has UPI Grown?
body.prompt: UPI handled about 2 crore transactions in FY17 and over 24,162 crore transactions in FY26. Roughly how many times larger is the FY26 figure? Round to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: 24,162 crore ÷ 2 crore = about 12,081 times. Demonetisation did not create UPI, which launched in April 2016, but the cash shortage pushed millions of Indians and small merchants to try digital payments for the first time, and most never went back.

body.title: Did Cash Disappear?
body.prompt: Currency in circulation was about ₹17.97 lakh crore just before demonetisation and about ₹42.85 lakh crore on 31 August 2026. How many times larger is it now? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: ₹42.85 lakh crore ÷ ₹17.97 lakh crore = 2.38 times. Despite the huge shift to digital payments, Indians hold far more cash today than before the note ban. Demonetisation changed the mix of payments much more than it changed the demand for cash.

children.text: What This Teaches About Central Banks
Three lessons stand out, and all three connect back to earlier chapters.

cells: Currency management is a core RBI function, not a footnote
Chapter 1: the six jobs of a central bank
Liquidity tools work in both directions: CRR, MSS and reverse repos can drain as easily as OMOs can inject
Chapter 2: CRR, and open market operations
A liquidity shock reaches asset prices fast, especially bonds
Chapter 3: why G-Sec yields react first

body.title: You Are a Bank Treasurer in November 2016
body.scenario: It is late November 2016. Your bank's deposits have jumped by thousands of crores in three weeks as customers deposit old notes. Loan demand is weak. The RBI has just imposed a 100% incremental CRR on the deposit growth since mid-September, which pays you nothing. Your CEO asks what to do with the money that is not impounded, and warns that much of these deposits may leave once withdrawal limits are lifted.
body.prompt: How would you deploy the surplus, and what risks would you flag?
body.modelAnswer: The key insight is that this money is temporary. Much of it will be withdrawn once cash is available again, so locking it into long-term loans or very long-dated bonds would create a mismatch. A sensible approach is to keep the surplus in short-dated government securities, treasury bills and the reverse repo window, staying liquid enough to fund withdrawals later. You would also flag three risks. First, duration risk: if you buy long bonds at these very low yields and rates rise later, you book mark-to-market losses. Second, the cost of the incremental CRR, which earns nothing, though the RBI signalled it was temporary and it was withdrawn from 10 December. Third, credit risk: many borrowers in cash-intensive businesses face a revenue shock, so loan repayments may weaken even as your deposits swell. The paradox of that moment was a bank flush with money and short of safe places to put it.

body.title: Go Deeper: What Is the Market Stabilisation Scheme?

children.text: The MSS was created in 2004 for a different problem: heavy foreign inflows forcing the RBI to buy dollars and release rupees. Under the scheme, the government issues special treasury bills and bonds whose proceeds are held in a separate account and not spent. The borrowing exists only to take money out of the system.

This matters because an ordinary OMO sale needs the RBI to hold bonds it can sell. In late 2016 the RBI did not have enough for the scale required, so raising the MSS ceiling from ₹30,000 crore to ₹6 lakh crore gave it a much bigger tool, at a cost borne by the government as interest on those securities.

cards.definition: The 8 November 2016 withdrawal of legal tender status from ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes, about 86% of currency value.
Money that must legally be accepted to settle a debt. Removing this status is what made the old notes unusable.
A temporary 100% reserve requirement on deposit growth in a set window, used in November 2016 to absorb surplus liquidity.
Special government securities issued purely to drain liquidity, with proceeds kept unspent.
The total value of notes and coins with the public and banks. About ₹42.85 lakh crore in August 2026.
Current account and savings account deposits, the cheapest funding for banks, which surged after demonetisation.
Unified Payments Interface, launched in April 2016, whose adoption accelerated sharply during the cash shortage.

body.label: RBI: Macroeconomic Impact of Demonetisation
body.description: The RBI's own preliminary assessment, covering the effects on deposits, liquidity, bond yields and the economy.

body.title: Trace the Liquidity Story Yourself
steps: Find the current currency in circulation figure in the RBI's weekly statistical supplement and compare it with ₹17.97 lakh crore
Look up a chart of the 10-year G-Sec yield from October 2016 to March 2017 and mark the demonetisation date
Check the latest monthly UPI transaction count published by NPCI
Compare a large bank's CASA ratio in FY16 with FY18 to see the deposit effect
Note how the incremental CRR of 2016 differs from the one used in August 2023, which you met in Chapter 2

points: Demonetisation removed legal tender status from ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes, about 86% of currency value, or ₹15.44 lakh crore.
Nearly all of it, about ₹15.28 lakh crore, came back into the banking system, according to the RBI Annual Report for 2016-17.
Deposits surged by roughly ₹6.72 lakh crore while loan demand stayed weak, so banks bought government bonds and yields fell sharply.
The RBI absorbed the flood with a temporary 100% incremental CRR, then replaced it with the MSS after its ceiling was raised to ₹6 lakh crore.
The RBI held the repo rate at 6.25% in December 2016, surprising markets that expected a cut.
Digital payments accelerated permanently, but cash did not disappear: currency in circulation is now well above its pre-2016 level.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not investment advice. It examines the monetary and market mechanics of demonetisation, not its political merits. Figures are as reported by the RBI and contemporary sources.
